query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, protective alumina-based (Al2O3) coating to a titanium‐ and nickel‐dominated single‐phase HEA will inhibit high-temperature oxidation, thereby preserving the alloy’s microstructural integrity and enhancing its elevated-temperature mechanical performance relative to an uncoated sample.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, cast or arc-melted HEA whose major constituents are titanium and nickel (with other elements balanced to form a stable solid solution), produced under standard processing conditions (e.g., vacuum or inert atmosphere melting) but without any special surface treatments.
generation.intervention: Deposit a uniform, thin (approximately 5–10 μm) alumina (Al2O3) coating using a method such as physical vapor deposition (PVD) or chemical vapor deposition (CVD) on the polished surface of the HEA.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing in air, for example, tensile or compressive tests at temperatures from 600 °C to 1000 °C (or a comparable extreme environment), including cyclic thermal loading to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The intact, oxidation-resistant alumina layer that protects the underlying HEA microstructure (grain boundaries and phase stability) from oxygen ingress and high-temperature degradation.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures in an oxidizing atmosphere, titanium is prone to form deleterious oxides that can weaken grain boundary bonding and reduce mechanical strength. The alumina coating serves as a diffusion barrier that minimizes oxygen penetration, thereby suppressing surface and grain-boundary oxidation, reducing phase segregation, and retaining solid solution strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated HEA samples will exhibit an increased yield strength and ultimate tensile strength along with improved ductility and reduced oxidation-induced degradation during high-temperature testing compared to uncoated samples.
generation.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-containing HEA processed without any additional surface coating.
generation.boundary: Applicable to HEAs where titanium and nickel are present in high proportions (typically >20 at.% each) and intended for use under elevated-temperature conditions in oxidizing atmospheres (e.g., 600–1000 °C). Results may not generalize to inert or reducing atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the mechanical performance improvement is uncertain; potential effects of coating adhesion, thermal expansion mismatch, and any coating-induced microstructural modifications are also unknown.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Ti-Ni-based HEA samples. Apply a 5–10 μm alumina coating via PVD or CVD on one set, leaving the other set uncoated. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature mechanical tests in air (for example, tensile tests at 800 °C) and to cyclic thermal loading for an extended period (e.g., 100 cycles). Post-test, characterize the oxidation layer thickness and microstructural integrity via SEM/EDS and TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (for example, at least a 10% increase in yield strength and reduced oxidation/degradation) compared to uncoated samples under the same test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
